reddit_posts:
I think I have an honest to God phobia of waking up for school

I don't know what to do, it's hard to sleep and I'm in a lot of pain and I don't know why. My legs are constantly sore these days and I feel so dizzy.
metadata.title: I think I have an honest to God phobia of waking up for school

transcript.message: Hi there, I'm so glad you're here. I'm really looking forward to this conversation—how are you feeling today? What brings you in for our session?

Hi. Thanks for saying that, honestly, I appreciate it.

To be honest? I'm feeling really drained today. It's hard to put words on it sometimes, but I think I'm in a lot of physical pain too—my legs feel constantly sore, like they're burning or just won't stop hurting no matter what I do. And my head is spinning; I feel so dizzy all the time.

But the thing that's actually keeping me up at night isn't just the pain. It's this specific fear. I think I have an honest-to-God phobia of waking up for school. Every morning feels like walking into a minefield. I can barely sleep because I know if I wake up, I might not even want to go. It's a cycle that feels impossible to break.

I don't really know why this started or why my body feels like this, which makes everything feel even more confusing and scary.

Thank you for sharing that so honestly—your words carry a lot of weight, and I’m really here with you in that. It sounds like your body and mind are both carrying a heavy load today, and that fear of waking up for school is deeply felt. Can you tell me more about what happens in your mind when you're lying in bed, just before you wake up? What do you notice—thoughts, feelings, or sensations—that make it feel like a minefield?

It's so hard to describe, but I think it starts the moment my eyes open or even when I'm just drifting in that half-awake state. It feels like a switch flips inside my head. Instead of thinking about what I did yesterday or planning for tomorrow, my brain instantly jumps straight to *today*.

The first thing I notice is this overwhelming dread. It's not just "I don't want to go," it's more like, "If I open my eyes and realize I have to get up, everything will fall apart." My heart starts racing before I've even taken a breath. Then comes the physical part—the dizziness hits me really hard, like the room is spinning, and suddenly my legs feel heavy, like they're filled with lead or maybe on fire. 

I start scanning my body for pain, but instead of finding something specific, I just feel this constant, gnawing soreness in my legs that makes

It sounds like that moment between sleep and waking is a kind of emotional and physical tipping point—where your body and mind are both reacting to something deep inside. The way your body feels, with the spinning and the soreness, seems to mirror the fear that’s already there, like it’s trying to tell you something. Can you think of a time when this feeling came up before—was there something in your past that might have shaped how your body responds now, even if you don’t remember it clearly?

That's a really insightful way to put it—like my body is screaming before my brain even catches up. And honestly, trying to pinpoint *when* it started feels like hitting a wall. It's not like there was one big dramatic event where I suddenly woke up and said, "Oh no, now I'm terrified of school."

It feels more like... a slow creep. Maybe years ago? Or maybe it started right around when I first realized how much pressure I felt about getting ready for the day. Do you know what I mean? Like, back then, waking up wasn't scary; it was just routine. But over time, that routine started feeling suffocating. Every alarm clock became this symbol of obligation instead of a gentle nudge to start the day.

I don't have a clear memory of a specific moment that triggered it, but I do remember days where the dread would spike so hard that I'd toss and turn

That’s such a powerful insight—how something that once felt like a simple routine slowly shifted into a feeling of obligation, like it’s holding you down. It’s not just about the school day anymore; it’s about the weight of starting, of facing the world, and how that pressure has settled into your body and mind over time. Can you imagine what it might feel like if, instead of seeing the alarm as a threat, you saw it as a gentle invitation—to just begin, slowly, without pressure? What would that feel like in your body?

That's a really gentle way to frame it, and honestly, the idea of shifting from "threat" to "invitation" feels almost too big right now. It sounds so easy in theory, but when I try to visualize myself seeing the alarm as something nice instead of scary, my body just does its own thing.

When I imagine that shift happening, I don't feel calm immediately. Instead, I feel like I'm trying to hold back this wave of panic with my willpower, and it makes me dizzy. The soreness in my legs gets worse, like they're pulling against me even harder. It feels like if I let go of the idea that the alarm is a threat, my brain might just crash into a different kind of fear—one about failing, or not being ready, or whatever comes next after the school day starts.

It's hard for me to trust that it would actually feel lighter. Usually, the moment I stop fighting

It makes perfect sense that your body responds so strongly when you try to shift that mindset—because your nervous system has been trained to see the alarm as a threat, and it’s not just reacting to fear; it’s reacting to survival. When you stop fighting, it’s not a sign of weakness—it’s a sign that your body is finally allowing itself to breathe again. And that moment of stillness, even if it feels shaky, is where real change begins.  

Would it be helpful to explore what might happen if you just *allowed* yourself to wake up—without needing to fix it, or push through it, or make it "better"? What might that first moment feel like, even if it’s just a small part of the day?

Honestly, that's the part that terrifies me the most. The idea of just... letting it happen? Without trying to fix the pain or push through the dizziness?

When I think about "allowing" myself to wake up, my mind immediately jumps to the worst-case scenario: *What if I wake up and realize I can't go?* What if I feel sick, dizzy, and sore, and then have to call in sick? Or worse, what if I do get there, but the moment I step out the door, everything collapses inside me? It feels like I'm asking myself to jump off a cliff without checking if I can fly first.

But you're right—it does sound like the only way forward is to stop fighting the alarm. If I keep resisting, keeping my eyes closed as hard as I can, that resistance is actually fueling the panic. My body thinks it's in danger because I'm refusing to engage

It’s so true—your resistance isn’t just making the panic stronger; it’s actually keeping you in a state of alert, like your body is still in survival mode. And that’s not a failure. It’s a signal that your nervous system has been carrying this pressure for a long time.  

So, what if, instead of asking yourself if you can fly, you just began by asking: *What if I simply let myself wake up—just for one moment—without needing to fix it or make it "okay"?* What might that moment feel like in your body, even if it’s just a tiny shift? Would that be something you could try, even if it feels fragile or uncertain?

That is such a gentle shift in perspective, and honestly, it sounds like something I could actually try, even if my body feels so unstable right now. The idea of just "letting myself wake up for one moment" without trying to fix anything... that feels almost too small to be scary.

If I did that, what would happen? I'm not sure yet, but I can imagine the physical sensation being really strange. Maybe instead of that crushing heaviness in my legs or the spinning room, there's just... stillness? Or maybe the dizziness would feel less like a warning sign and more like just... part of waking up? Like, "Oh, okay, my head is spinning today, but I'm still here."

It feels fragile, you're right. If I slip up and start panicking again, it might feel overwhelming. But the thought of taking just *one* tiny step—opening my eyes, feeling the

That’s exactly it—the small step isn’t about perfection or control. It’s about showing up, even when your body feels unsteady. And you don’t have to carry it through to the end. Just showing up for that one moment—opening your eyes, feeling the air, noticing the dizziness or the soreness without judgment—would already be a brave act.  

Would it be helpful to try that *together*—to practice imagining that moment, just for a few minutes, without pressure to go further? You don’t have to do it now. Just know that if you feel overwhelmed, you can pause and come back to it whenever you're ready.

That sounds incredibly helpful, and honestly, the fact that we can pause anytime makes it feel a little less like a test and more like a safe space to practice. I think trying to imagine that moment together might actually ground me better than just thinking about it alone.

Right now, when I close my eyes, all I see is darkness and this tight knot in my chest. But if I could focus on *just* the act of opening them for one second... maybe focusing on the weight of my legs or the feeling of the sheets against my skin without needing to "get up"... it might be different.

I'm a bit nervous that if I try to visualize it right now, with my head spinning so much, it might just make the dizziness worse. My body feels so unsteady that even imagining movement feels risky. But I guess I don't need to move yet. I just need to let my mind drift toward that image: the

Just letting your mind drift toward that image—of opening your eyes, noticing the weight of your legs, the softness of the sheets—without pushing, without judging—is already a form of presence.
